skills.name: Show a linear inequality as a region (half plane) on a graph

note.text:
A line divides the plane into two half planes. An inequality such as y ≤ 2x + 1 describes one of them.
1. Draw the boundary line y = 2x + 1: solid if the line is included (≤, ≥), broken if not (<, >).
2. Test a point not on the line, usually O(0, 0): 0 ≤ 1 is true, so O is in the wanted region.
3. Shade the unwanted side (the convention in GCE answers), leaving the wanted region clear.
x ≥ 3 is the region to the right of the vertical line x = 3; y < −1 is below the horizontal line y = −1.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to draw the region for a linear inequality: the right boundary (solid or broken) and the right side, tested with a point.
Builds on: Lesson {20} (drawing lines) and Lesson {16} (inequalities).
Leads to: Lesson {22} (regions for several inequalities) and linear programming in Form Five.

sections.heading: Boundary and side
sections.text:
The inequality y ≤ {mono(2, 'x')} + {1} is true for the points on the line y = {mono(2, 'x')} + {1} and for every point on one side of it.
• Boundary: draw the line. With ≤ or ≥ it is included, so draw it solid. With < or > draw it broken.
• Side: test a point that is not on the line. O({0}, {0}): {0} ≤ {mono(2, 'x')} + {1} becomes {0} ≤ {1}, true. So O's side is wanted.
• Shade the unwanted side. The clear region shows all the solutions.

sections.heading: Vertical and horizontal boundaries
sections.text:
x ≥ {3}: the boundary is the vertical line x = {3}; the wanted region is to the right of it.
y < {-1}: the boundary is the horizontal line y = {-1}, broken; the wanted region is below it.
If the line passes through O, test another point such as ({1}, {0}).
Some books shade the wanted region instead. Always say which convention you use; here the shaded part is unwanted.

key_words.meaning: all the points on one side of a line
the line that separates the two sides
the part shaded because it does not satisfy the inequality

examples: x + y < {4}: broken line x + y = {4}; O is wanted
y ≥ {-2}: solid horizontal line; wanted above

mistake.wrong: y < x + {2}: draw the line solid
mistake.right: y < x + {2}: draw the line broken
mistake.why: < leaves out the equals case, so the points on the line are not solutions.

steps: Boundary y = {poly([m, 'x'], [c, ''])}: x = {0}, y = {c}; x = {1}, y = {m + c}. ≤ includes the line, so draw it solid.
Test O({0}, {0}): {0} ≤ {c} is true, so O is in the wanted region.
Shade the other side, above the line: that is the unwanted region.
worked_example.answer: the unshaded region below the solid line y = {poly([m, 'x'], [c, ''])}

cards.idea: ≤ and ≥ include the line: draw it solid. < and > leave it out: draw it broken.
example: y < x + {2}: broken line; y ≥ x + {2}: solid line

cards.idea: Test a point such as O({0}, {0}): if it makes the inequality true, it is in the wanted region.
example: y ≤ {mono(2, 'x')} + {1}: {0} ≤ {1} is true, so O is wanted

cards.idea: Shade the unwanted side; the clear region is the solution.
example: for y ≤ {mono(2, 'x')} + {1}, shade above the line

check.prompt: The graph shows a line and a shaded (unwanted) region. Which inequality describes the unshaded region?

misconceptions.explain: The shading is the unwanted side. The clear region is {below ? 'below' : 'above'} the line.
Look at the line: {strict ? 'broken, so it is not included' : 'solid, so it is included'}.
The line slopes {m > 0 ? 'up' : 'down'} to the right, so its gradient is {m}.

solution: The boundary is y = {poly([m, 'x'], [c, ''])}, drawn {strict ? 'broken (not included)' : 'solid (included)'}.
The clear region is {below ? 'below' : 'above'} the line.

questions.prompt: When you draw the boundary of {mono(a, 'x')} + {mono(b, 'y')} {op} {c} on a graph, how should the line be drawn?
questions.correct: {op == '<' || op == '>' ? 'Broken, because the line itself is not included' : 'Solid, because the line itself is included'}

distractors.text: {op == '<' || op == '>' ? 'Solid, because the line itself is included' : 'Broken, because the line itself is not included'}
Solid, because every boundary is drawn solid
{op == '<' || op == '>' ? 'Broken, because the region is below the line' : 'Solid, because the region is above the line'}

misconceptions.explain: ≤ and ≥ include the line (solid); < and > do not (broken).
A boundary that is not part of the solution is drawn broken.
Solid or broken depends on whether the line is included, not on which side the region is.

solution: {op} {op == '<' || op == '>' ? 'leaves out the equals case' : 'includes the equals case'}.

questions.prompt: Is the point ({px}, {py}) in the region y {op} {poly([m, 'x'], [c, ''])}?
questions.correct: {holds(py, op, m * px + c) ? 'Yes: ' + fmt(py) + ' ' + op + ' ' + fmt(m * px + c) + ' is true' : 'No: ' + fmt(py) + ' ' + op + ' ' + fmt(m * px + c) + ' is false'}

distractors.text: {holds(py, op, m * px + c) ? 'No: ' + fmt(py) + ' ' + op + ' ' + fmt(m * px + c) + ' is false' : 'Yes: ' + fmt(py) + ' ' + op + ' ' + fmt(m * px + c) + ' is true'}
Yes: every point with a positive x is in it
No: points on the boundary are never included

misconceptions.explain: Substitute and compare: {py} {op} {m * px + c} is {holds(py, op, m * px + c) ? 'true' : 'false'}.
Whether a point is in the region depends on the inequality, not just on x.
With ≤ or ≥ the boundary is included. Substitute and compare.

solution: Compare with y = {py}: is {py} {op} {m * px + c}? {holds(py, op, m * px + c) ? 'Yes.' : 'No.'}

questions.prompt: The graph shows the region {v == 'x' ? 'beside a vertical line' : 'beside a horizontal line'}. The unshaded part is wanted. Which inequality describes it?

misconceptions.explain: The shaded side is unwanted; the wanted side is where {v} is {op == '<' || op == '≤' ? 'smaller' : 'larger'} than {k}.
The line is {strict ? 'broken: not included' : 'solid: included'}.

solution: The boundary is the {v == 'x' ? 'vertical' : 'horizontal'} line {v} = {k}, drawn {strict ? 'broken' : 'solid'}.
The clear side is where {v} is {op == '<' || op == '≤' ? 'smaller' : 'larger'}.

questions.prompt: To show {mono(a, 'x')} + {mono(b, 'y')} {op} {c} you draw the line {mono(a, 'x')} + {mono(b, 'y')} = {c}. Which side do you shade (unwanted)?
questions.correct: {holds(0, op, c) ? 'The side that does not contain O(0, 0), because O satisfies the inequality' : 'The side that contains O(0, 0), because O does not satisfy the inequality'}

distractors.text: {holds(0, op, c) ? 'The side that contains O(0, 0), because O satisfies the inequality' : 'The side that does not contain O(0, 0), because O does not satisfy the inequality'}
Always the side above the line

misconceptions.explain: If O satisfies the inequality, O's side is wanted and stays clear.
'Above' depends on the inequality. Test a point such as O.
O's side is shaded only if O does not satisfy the inequality.

solution: Test O: {a} × {0} + {b} × {0} = {0}, and {0} {op} {c} is {holds(0, op, c) ? 'true' : 'false'}.
{holds(0, op, c) ? 'O is wanted, so shade the other side.' : 'O is unwanted, so shade its side.'}
